key_insight: This paper shows that large language models can help automate reproducibility checks in the social and behavioral sciences by comparing model-generated analyses to original study findings. The approach offers a scalable alternative to labor-intensive human reanalysis.
problem_solved: Traditional reproducibility assessments require independent researchers to reanalyze original data, which is time-consuming, costly, and hard to scale across many published studies.
method: Selected 76 published studies with predefined claims from the social and behavioral sciences.
Used large language models to generate analyses for the studies and compare the outputs with the original reported findings.
Evaluated how well LLM-based assessments could recover or match reproducibility outcomes relative to the original analyses.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests LLMs can be used as practical assistants for meta-research and research integrity workflows. It points toward faster, cheaper screening of reproducibility at scale, though human oversight remains important.
visual_elements: Flow diagram: original study -> LLM analysis -> reproducibility comparison
Side-by-side comparison chart of original findings vs. LLM-generated findings
Icon set showing scalability, speed, and automation
Bar chart summarizing agreement/recovery rates across studies
paper_title: Automated reproducibility assessments in the social and behavioral sciences using large language models
paper_authors: Tobias Holtdirk, Pietro Marcolongo, Anna Steinberg Schulten, Felix Henninger, Stefan Rose
